verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Agra footwear MSMEs with clean GST and tight monthly stock reporting; avoid sub-scale job-work units with no branded or institutional buyer.
title: Agra Footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Agra footwear is a low-capex, labour-heavy assembly trade: soles, uppers, adhesives and lining go in, finished pairs come out, and cash comes back only after the trade channel sells through. **The industry does not have a capital-intensive manufacturing process and entry barriers remain low [10], so your real risk is not the factory, it is the buyer list and the stock.** Because capex is small, a unit can scale output fast on borrowed working capital; that is exactly where over-lending happens.

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits in design, brand and distribution, not stitching. Peers show the split: Relaxo Q4 FY26 revenue INR751 crore, EBITDA margin 16.5% [5], while a regional manufacturer-retailer runs 116 showrooms and 49 franchisees [8]. **The manufacturer with a brand keeps the margin; the job-worker keeps a conversion charge.** So when a proposal lands, check who the top five buyers are and what share they hold; if one buyer is above a third of sales, ask for that buyer's payment history and past-due record.

## What has changed now
Two things. First, the GST cut from 12% to 5% caused downstocking, then recovery, with distributor count rising from 550 to 630 in one quarter [4] — **so ask for the last six months of GST returns, not the last quarter, to see whether the recovery is real or a restock bounce.** Second, SIDBI and AFMEC have signed an MoU for financial and technical support to Agra footwear MSMEs [1][2][3]; that is local news, dated 29-30 October 2026, and it is a funding channel, not a credit signal. Peer results are healthy (Bata Q1FY27 net profit Rs 64 crore, up 23% [6]) but they are large branded players, not Agra units.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
UP GST collections are running +14.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], so the state demand pool is expanding faster than the country. **Pursue component makers and branded/licensed manufacturers with repeat institutional buyers; avoid pure job-work units with one buyer and no design function.** Structure as cash-flow lending against stock and receivables, not land. Take monthly GST returns, stock statements and a buyer-wise ageing every month; if stock cover exceeds 90 days of sales, cut limit and ask for the slow-moving SKU list.

## Early warning signs
Watch three things monthly: GST turnover falling while bank turnover holds (diversion), receivable days stretching beyond the stated credit terms, and stock that does not move. **If a unit's GST-paid sales drop two months running while its limit utilisation rises, freeze fresh disbursal and inspect godown stock.** Note that the rating reports [8][9][10] are undated or old and describe other entities; treat them as sector colour only. Agra-specific published data is thin, so lean on first principles and these peers.
watch: GST sales fall 2 months while utilisation rises -> freeze disbursal, inspect stock
Stock cover above 90 days of sales -> cut limit, demand slow-moving SKU list
Top buyer above one-third of sales -> seek buyer payment record, cap exposure
Days stretch beyond agreed credit terms -> move to cash/LC terms
Utilisation above 90% with flat sales -> no enhancement, review drawing power
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
news_why: SIDBI-AFMEC MoU is a funding channel; peer results firm but not Agra-specific.
